Title: Analysis of the Supervisory Commission's Authority Scope under the National Supervision Law and Its Division of Responsibilities with Judicial Organs

Abstract

The establishment of the Supervisory Commission is one of the most consequential institutional changes in China's constitutional and legal order since the reform and opening-up period. It has transformed the previous fragmented anti-corruption system into a unified national supervision system and has created a new constitutional organ that exercises supervisory power independently. This paper examines the authority scope of the Supervisory Commission under the Supervision Law of the People's Republic of China, with particular attention to the division of responsibilities between supervisory commissions and judicial organs, including people's procuratorates, people's courts, and public security organs. It first explains the constitutional and legislative background of the Supervisory Commission, then analyzes its three core powers of supervision, investigation, and disposition. It next considers the constitutional and statutory interfaces between supervisory power and procuratorial, adjudicatory, and public-security power. It then identifies key issues and controversies, including jurisdictional overlap over duty-related crimes, the treatment of judicial staff misconduct, evidentiary conversion, the legal status of detention, defense rights, and the problem of supervising the supervisor. The paper concludes that the Supervision Law has established a workable but still incomplete framework and recommends clearer jurisdictional rules, stronger procedural safeguards, more robust evidentiary standards, improved coordination mechanisms, and more effective external oversight.

I. Introduction: Background and Legislative Significance

The creation of the Supervisory Commission was not a routine administrative reform. It was a constitutional reconstruction of the state's anti-corruption and supervision architecture. Before 2018, anti-corruption functions were dispersed among the discipline inspection system of the Communist Party of China, administrative supervisory organs under the government, and the prosecutorial system's anti-corruption and anti-malfeasance departments. This arrangement produced overlapping jurisdictions, duplicated investigations, inconsistent evidentiary standards, and occasional difficulties in converting disciplinary evidence into criminal evidence. The 2018 constitutional amendment added a new section on supervisory commissions to the Constitution, and the Supervision Law of the People's Republic of China was enacted to implement that constitutional design. The National Supervision Commission was established as the highest supervisory organ, and local supervisory commissions were established at corresponding levels. The Constitution provides that supervisory commissions at all levels are state supervisory organs, that the National Supervision Commission leads local supervisory commissions, and that higher-level supervisory commissions lead lower-level ones. The Supervision Law further specifies that supervisory commissions are specialized organs exercising national supervision functions and that they supervise all public officials who exercise public power.

The legislative significance of this change is threefold. First, it unified the supervision of public officials. The Supervision Law expanded the scope of supervision from administrative organs and their personnel to all public officials exercising public power, including personnel in Party organs, people's congresses, government organs, political consultative conferences, courts, procuratorates, public institutions, state-owned enterprises, grassroots organizations, and other entities exercising public functions. This represents the principle of comprehensive coverage of public power. Second, it constitutionalized supervisory power. Supervisory commissions are not administrative organs subordinate to governments, nor are they judicial organs. They are constitutional organs with independent constitutional status. Article 125 of the Constitution states that supervisory commissions exercise supervisory power independently according to law and are not subject to interference by administrative organs, social organizations, or individuals. Third, it created a new power relationship among supervisory, procuratorial, adjudicatory, and law-enforcement organs. Article 127 of the Constitution provides that supervisory organs shall, in handling cases of official misconduct and duty-related crimes, cooperate with and check judicial organs, procuratorial organs, and law-enforcement departments, and that relevant organs and units shall provide assistance when supervisory organs need it according to law. This formula of cooperation and checking is the constitutional foundation for the division of responsibilities discussed in this paper.

The Supervision Law's core provisions reflect this design. Article 3 defines supervisory commissions as specialized organs exercising national supervision functions, legally supervising all public officials exercising public power, investigating official misconduct and duty-related crimes, carrying out clean governance and anti-corruption work, and upholding the dignity of the Constitution and laws. Article 4 provides that supervisory commissions independently exercise supervisory power according to law, free from interference by administrative organs, social organizations, and individuals, and that in handling cases of official misconduct and duty-related crimes, supervisory organs shall cooperate with and check judicial organs, procuratorial organs, and law-enforcement departments. Article 10 establishes the leadership relationship between the National Supervision Commission and local supervisory commissions and between higher-level and lower-level supervisory commissions. These provisions are not merely organizational; they define the institutional logic within which the boundaries between supervisory and judicial functions must be drawn.

The academic and practical importance of this topic lies in the fact that the Supervision Law is a framework law. It establishes the main institutions and powers but leaves many operational details to implementing regulations, internal rules, and practice. The interface between supervisory investigation and criminal procedure is particularly sensitive because supervisory investigation is not governed by the Criminal Procedure Law in the same way as public-security investigation or procuratorial investigation. The transfer of a case from a supervisory commission to a people's procuratorate marks a critical transition from supervisory procedure to criminal procedure. How evidence is converted, how defense rights are protected, how jurisdiction is allocated, and how courts review transferred cases are questions that directly affect the credibility and legitimacy of the anti-corruption system. This paper therefore treats the division of responsibilities not as a narrow technical issue but as a constitutional and rule-of-law issue.

II. Analysis of the Authority Scope of the Supervisory Commission

The authority of the Supervisory Commission is best understood through its three core functions: supervision, investigation, and disposition. These functions are related but distinct. Supervision is preventive and continuous; investigation is reactive and case-based; disposition is corrective and punitive. The Supervision Law grants supervisory commissions the power to perform all three, subject to constitutional and statutory limits.

A. Supervision Power

Supervision is the primary function of the Supervisory Commission. Under Article 11 of the Supervision Law, supervisory commissions supervise public officials' performance of duties, their use of public power, their integrity and ethical conduct, and their compliance with laws and regulations. The purpose is not to replace ordinary administrative management or internal discipline but to ensure that public power is exercised lawfully, fairly, and cleanly. The scope of supervision is defined by the concept of the public official exercising public power. Article 15 of the Supervision Law enumerates categories of public officials, including personnel of state organs, personnel of Party and state organs, personnel of state-owned enterprises, personnel of public institutions, personnel of grassroots self-governance organizations, and others who exercise public power according to law. This broad scope is consistent with the principle of comprehensive supervision and with the constitutional position of supervisory commissions as organs supervising all public power.

The supervision power includes several subsidiary powers. Supervisory commissions may conduct routine supervision, receive reports and complaints, conduct conversations and inquiries, require explanations, inspect work, and issue supervisory recommendations. They may also establish supervisory offices in certain organs or regions. These powers are preventive and educational in nature. They are not criminal investigation powers, although information obtained through supervision may later become relevant to an investigation. The distinction matters because supervision measures are generally less intrusive than investigation measures and are subject to different procedural safeguards. The Supervision Law emphasizes that supervision should be exercised according to law and that supervisory organs should accept supervision themselves. This internal tension between broad supervisory reach and the need for self-restraint is a recurring theme in the implementation of the law.

B. Investigation Power

The investigation power is the most coercive and most debated power of the Supervisory Commission. Under the Supervision Law, supervisory commissions investigate official misconduct and duty-related crimes involving corruption, bribery, abuse of power, dereliction of duty, power rent-seeking, transfer of benefits, favoritism, and waste of state resources. These categories correspond broadly to the crimes defined in Chapters VIII and IX of the Criminal Law, including embezzlement, bribery, abuse of power, dereliction of duty, and related offenses. The investigation power is not a general criminal investigation power. It is limited to duty-related crimes committed by public officials in the exercise of public power or in connection with their official positions. Ordinary crimes such as intentional homicide, theft, fraud, drug offenses, or traffic offenses are investigated by public security organs under the Criminal Procedure Law, even if the suspect happens to be a public official.

The Supervision Law grants supervisory commissions a range of investigation measures. These include interrogation, questioning, inquiry, inspection, examination, search, seizure, freezing, appraisal, and detention in a designated place, known as liuzhi. The most significant is liuzhi, which replaced the earlier shuanggui practice and is intended to be a lawful supervisory measure rather than an extralegal disciplinary measure. Liuzhi is subject to statutory conditions, approval procedures, and time limits. It is not a criminal compulsory measure under the Criminal Procedure Law, and it is not ordered by a procuratorate or a court. This distinction is central to the debate over procedural safeguards. During liuzhi, the person is not formally a criminal suspect under the Criminal Procedure Law, and defense counsel generally does not have the same access as in ordinary criminal proceedings. Once the case is transferred to the procuratorate, criminal procedure begins, and the suspect acquires the procedural rights of a criminal suspect.

The Supervision Law also addresses evidence. Evidence collected by supervisory organs according to law may be used in criminal proceedings. This provision is necessary because the procuratorate and the court must rely on the supervisory investigation record when prosecuting and trying the case. However, it also raises questions about evidentiary standards. If supervisory evidence is to be used in a criminal trial, it should meet the standards of relevance, legality, authenticity, and voluntariness required by the Criminal Procedure Law. The Supervision Law and related rules prohibit the collection of evidence by torture, violence, threat, enticement, deceit, or other illegal methods, and illegal evidence should be excluded. The practical challenge is to ensure that the exclusionary rule is applied effectively across the supervisory-criminal interface.

C. Disposition Power

The disposition power is the power to make legal consequences follow from supervision and investigation. Under the Supervision Law, supervisory commissions may take measures against public officials who violate laws and regulations. These measures include administrative disciplinary sanctions such as warnings, demerits, major demerits, demotion, removal from office, and dismissal. They may also include supervisory recommendations, criticism and education, orders to make corrections, and decisions to recover or confiscate illicit gains. For public officials suspected of duty-related crimes, supervisory commissions transfer the investigation results to people's procuratorates for review and prosecution. The transfer decision is a pivotal act. It does not itself determine criminal guilt; it initiates the procuratorial review stage. The procuratorate then decides whether to prosecute, whether to return the case for supplementary investigation, or whether to decline prosecution. If the procuratorate decides not to prosecute, it must notify the supervisory commission, and the supervisory commission may invoke statutory reconsideration or review procedures.

The disposition power also includes internal accountability and the power to issue supervisory recommendations to the units concerned. These recommendations can require the unit to correct management problems, improve systems, and hold relevant personnel accountable. This preventive dimension is often overlooked in discussions focused on criminal prosecution, but it is essential to the Supervision Law's broader anti-corruption strategy. The law aims not only to punish wrongdoing but also to improve governance and reduce opportunities for corruption.

D. Constitutional and Criminal Procedure Law Interfaces

The Constitution does not use the language of criminal investigation when describing supervisory power. It states that supervisory commissions exercise the functions and powers of supervision, investigation, and disposition according to law. The Constitution also states that supervisory organs shall cooperate with and check judicial organs, procuratorial organs, and law-enforcement departments. This means that the relationship between supervisory and judicial organs is not one of hierarchy but of constitutional division of labor. The supervisory commission is not superior to the procuratorate or the court, and the procuratorate and court are not superior to the supervisory commission. Each exercises its own constitutional function.

The Criminal Procedure Law is the basic law governing criminal investigations, prosecution, trial, and enforcement. It does not grant the Supervisory Commission its supervisory, investigative, or disposition powers; those powers come from the Constitution and the Supervision Law. The Criminal Procedure Law instead regulates the interface between supervisory investigation and criminal prosecution. Article 19 of the Criminal Procedure Law assigns ordinary criminal investigation to public security organs, subject to exceptions. It also preserves a limited investigative jurisdiction for people's procuratorates over crimes committed by judicial staff in litigation, such as abuse of power and dereliction of duty, and over certain major duty-related crimes when the procuratorate considers it necessary and the conditions are met. Article 170 of the Criminal Procedure Law addresses cases transferred by supervisory organs for prosecution. It requires the procuratorate to review the case according to law and to decide whether to prosecute. If the evidence is insufficient or the facts are unclear, the procuratorate may return the case to the supervisory organ for supplementary investigation. If the procuratorate decides not to prosecute, it must notify the supervisory organ. These provisions create a procedural bridge between the Supervision Law and the Criminal Procedure Law.

The interface is not complete. The Criminal Procedure Law's investigative supervision provisions, which allow the procuratorate to supervise public-security investigations, do not apply in the same way to supervisory investigations. The procuratorate's check on supervisory investigation occurs primarily through the review-for-prosecution stage, not through real-time investigative supervision. The court's check occurs at trial, where the court examines the evidence and the legality of the procedure. This design reflects the constitutional independence of supervisory power, but it also creates gaps that require careful institutional design.

III. Division of Responsibilities between Supervisory Commissions and Judicial Organs

The division of responsibilities between supervisory commissions and judicial organs can be analyzed along three axes: the procuratorate, the court, and the public security organ. Each relationship has its own constitutional basis, statutory rules, and practical challenges.

A. Supervisory Commissions and People's Procuratorates

The people's procuratorate is both a legal supervision organ and a criminal prosecution organ. Its relationship with the supervisory commission is the most direct and the most complex. In the anti-corruption process, the supervisory commission investigates duty-related crimes, and the procuratorate reviews the case for prosecution. The procuratorate does not direct the supervisory investigation, nor does it have the power to order the supervisory commission to investigate or not investigate a particular case. The supervisory commission's investigative independence is constitutionally protected. However, the procuratorate's review is not a formality. It must examine whether the facts are clear, whether the evidence is sufficient, whether the legal elements of the crime are met, and whether the procedure was lawful. If the evidence is insufficient, the procuratorate may return the case for supplementary investigation. If the case does not meet the conditions for prosecution, the procuratorate may decide not to prosecute. This is the principal check on supervisory investigation.

There is also a jurisdictional overlap between the two organs. The supervisory commission has general jurisdiction over duty-related crimes of public officials, including corruption, bribery, abuse of power, and dereliction of duty. The procuratorate has limited jurisdiction under Article 19 of the Criminal Procedure Law over judicial staff who abuse power or commit dereliction of duty in litigation. This creates a potential overlap when a judge or procurator is suspected of accepting bribes in exchange for a favorable ruling or of abusing power in handling a case. Is the case a bribery case within the supervisory commission's jurisdiction, or an abuse-of-power case within the procuratorate's jurisdiction? The answer depends on the nature of the alleged conduct. If the core allegation is taking money or property in exchange for official action, the supervisory commission has jurisdiction over bribery. If the core allegation is abuse of power or dereliction of duty in litigation without a bribery element, the procuratorate may have jurisdiction. In practice, cases often involve both elements, and coordination is necessary. The supervising commission may lead the investigation of the duty-related crime, while the procuratorate handles the litigation-related misconduct. Clear rules are needed to prevent either duplication or gaps.

The procuratorate also has a role in supervising the legality of criminal proceedings after the case is transferred. It can review the evidence, interview the suspect, and decide whether to prosecute. But it cannot supervise the supervisory commission's investigation in the same way it supervises public-security investigation. This asymmetry is a deliberate constitutional design, but it has prompted calls for a more robust review mechanism. Some scholars propose that the procuratorate should be allowed to intervene earlier in major cases, or that a separate review procedure should be established for supervisory investigative measures that significantly restrict personal liberty. Others argue that early intervention would compromise the independence of supervisory power. The debate is unresolved and is likely to remain central to future reforms.

B. Supervisory Commissions and People's Courts

The people's court is the adjudicatory organ. Its relationship with the supervisory commission is indirect but constitutionally significant. The court does not investigate duty-related crimes and does not direct the supervisory commission. Its role is to try cases that the procuratorate has prosecuted after supervisory investigation. In doing so, the court must apply the Criminal Procedure Law's standards of proof and evidence. It must determine whether the defendant's guilt is proven beyond a reasonable doubt. It must examine the legality of the evidence and exclude illegally obtained evidence. It must protect the defendant's right to defense and ensure a fair trial. These judicial functions are not a review of the supervisory commission's policy decisions, but they are a review of the legal sufficiency of the case that the supervisory commission has produced.

The court's check is therefore real but limited. The court cannot declare a supervisory investigation unlawful in the abstract, nor can it order the supervisory commission to change its internal practices. It can, however, acquit a defendant if the evidence is insufficient, exclude evidence if it was illegally obtained, and sentence according to law if guilt is proven. In serious duty-related crime cases, courts have generally accepted supervisory evidence and have convicted defendants after trial. The Lai Xiaomin case is illustrative. Lai Xiaomin, a former senior executive of a state-owned financial institution, was investigated by the National Supervision Commission, transferred to the procuratorate for prosecution, and tried by a people's court. The case demonstrated the full chain from supervisory investigation to procuratorial review to judicial trial. It also showed that the court retains the power to determine guilt and sentence, even though the investigation was conducted by a supervisory organ. The case did not resolve all jurisdictional and evidentiary questions, but it confirmed that the constitutional design contemplates a real trial stage, not a mere ratification of the investigation.

The court's role is also affected by the trial-centered criminal procedure reform. This reform requires that facts be ascertained and evidence be examined in court, that witnesses testify in court when necessary, and that the court's judgment be based on the evidence presented at trial. Applying this reform to supervisory-transferred cases is challenging because much of the evidence is produced during the supervisory investigation, and witnesses may have already given statements to the supervisory commission. The court must decide how to handle inconsistencies, how to assess the voluntariness of statements, and how to ensure that the defendant can confront the evidence against him. These are not abstract concerns; they go to the heart of the fairness of the proceedings.

C. Supervisory Commissions and Public Security Organs

The public security organ is the main criminal investigation organ for ordinary crimes. Its relationship with the supervisory commission is based on the distinction between duty-related crimes and ordinary crimes. If a public official is suspected of corruption or bribery, the supervisory commission investigates. If the same person is suspected of an ordinary crime such as intentional injury, theft, or illegal possession of firearms, the public security organ investigates. If the two types of crime are connected, the organs must coordinate. For example, a public official may accept bribes and also commit money laundering. The supervisory commission investigates the bribery, and the public security organ investigates the money laundering. The cases may be handled separately or jointly, depending on the circumstances. The key principle is that each organ should exercise its own statutory jurisdiction and that neither should substitute for the other.

There are practical areas of cooperation. Supervisory commissions may need public security assistance in locating suspects, executing detention, maintaining order, conducting forensic examinations, or handling traffic and communication records. The Supervision Law provides that relevant organs and units shall provide assistance when supervisory organs need it according to law. This assistance is not a delegation of supervisory power; it is operational support. The public security organ remains responsible for its own investigation and must comply with the Criminal Procedure Law. The boundary is important because public-security measures such as criminal detention and arrest are governed by the Criminal Procedure Law and require procuratorial approval or court decision in certain circumstances, whereas supervisory measures such as liuzhi are governed by the Supervision Law.

D. Cooperation Mechanisms

The Supervision Law and related rules establish several cooperation mechanisms. These include case transfer, information sharing, joint meetings, evidence conversion, asset recovery, and international cooperation. Case transfer is the most formal. When the supervisory commission completes its investigation and decides to transfer the case for prosecution, it must transfer the case file, evidence, and relevant materials to the procuratorate. The procuratorate then reviews the case and decides whether to prosecute. If supplementary investigation is needed, the case is returned to the supervisory commission. If the procuratorate decides not to prosecute, it must notify the supervisory commission and explain the reasons. The supervisory commission may request reconsideration or review through statutory channels.

Information sharing is less formal but equally important. Supervisory commissions, procuratorates, courts, and public security organs may need to share information about public officials, cases, and trends. However, information sharing must respect confidentiality, personal data protection, and the principle of necessity. Joint meetings and coordination committees can help resolve jurisdictional disputes and improve consistency. Evidence conversion is a central practical issue. Evidence collected by the supervisory commission must be presented in a form that the procuratorate and court can use. This requires proper documentation, chain of custody, and compliance with legal standards. Asset recovery requires coordination among supervisory, procuratorial, judicial, public-security, foreign-affairs, and financial authorities. International cooperation, including extradition and mutual legal assistance, requires the supervisory commission to work through the central authorities designated under China's international legal obligations.

IV. Key Issues and Controversies

The implementation of the Supervision Law has generated several unresolved issues. These issues are not merely technical; they reflect deeper tensions between supervisory efficacy and procedural justice, between constitutional independence and accountability, and between comprehensive coverage and jurisdictional clarity.

A. The Nature of Supervisory Power and the Limits of Jurisdiction

The first controversy concerns the nature of supervisory power. Is supervisory investigation a form of criminal investigation? The Supervision Law does not say so. It treats supervisory investigation as a distinct constitutional function. The Criminal Procedure Law does not apply to supervisory investigation in the same way it applies to public-security investigation. This distinction has advantages: it allows the supervisory commission to act independently and to avoid the procedural constraints that might hamper anti-corruption work. But it also creates a gap. If supervisory investigation is not criminal investigation, what procedural safeguards apply? The Supervision Law provides some safeguards, but they are less detailed than those in the Criminal Procedure Law. The risk is that a person may be subjected to significant coercive measures without the full protections of criminal procedure.

This issue is connected to the broader question of jurisdictional limits. The supervisory commission's investigation power is limited to duty-related crimes. But the line between duty-related and ordinary crimes is not always clear. For example, a public official who uses his position to embezzle public funds commits a duty-related crime. A public official who uses his position to facilitate a private business deal may commit both a duty-related crime and an ordinary crime. The supervisory commission and the public security organ may both have jurisdiction. Without clear rules, there is a risk of jurisdictional competition, delayed case handling, or duplication of investigative measures. A case-allocation mechanism based on the primary nature of the alleged conduct, the stage of the investigation, and the seriousness of the offense would help. Where the duty-related and ordinary crimes are inextricably linked, a joint case-handling mechanism led by the organ with the primary jurisdiction, with assistance from the other, may be appropriate.

B. Judicial Staff Misconduct and the Procuratorate's Residual Jurisdiction

The second controversy concerns judicial staff misconduct. Article 19 of the Criminal Procedure Law preserves a limited investigative jurisdiction for procuratorates over judicial staff who abuse power or commit dereliction of duty in litigation. This jurisdiction is an exception to the supervisory commission's general jurisdiction over duty-related crimes. The rationale is that the procuratorate, as the legal supervision organ, is best positioned to investigate misconduct within the judicial process. But the boundary is unclear. If a judge accepts a bribe and then abuses power in a ruling, the case involves both bribery and abuse of power. The supervisory commission has jurisdiction over bribery, and the procuratorate may have jurisdiction over abuse of power in litigation. Which organ should lead? If both investigate separately, there may be inconsistent findings and wasted resources. If one organ leads, the other may feel that its statutory jurisdiction is being undermined.

A possible solution is to adopt a primary-conduct test. If the alleged misconduct is primarily economic corruption, the supervisory commission should lead. If it is primarily a distortion of the litigation process without a bribery element, the procuratorate should lead. If the two are inseparable, the supervisory commission should lead the corruption investigation, and the procuratorate should provide assistance on litigation-related issues. The results should be shared, and the case should be transferred to the procuratorate for unified prosecution where appropriate. This approach respects both jurisdictions and avoids duplication. It also requires a formal dispute-resolution mechanism, such as a joint meeting at the provincial level or a designation by the higher-level supervisory commission and procuratorate.

C. Evidence Conversion and Evidentiary Standards

The third controversy concerns evidence. The Supervision Law allows evidence collected by supervisory organs to be used in criminal proceedings. But the standards for collecting, preserving, and presenting that evidence are not identical to those in the Criminal Procedure Law. This creates a risk that evidence may be admitted in court without adequate scrutiny. The exclusionary rule is the main safeguard. If evidence is obtained through torture, violence, threat, enticement, deceit, or other illegal methods, it should be excluded. But applying the exclusionary rule to supervisory evidence requires the court to examine the supervisory investigation record, which may be difficult if the record is incomplete or if the investigators are not available for cross-examination.

A related issue is the treatment of witness statements and confessions. In ordinary criminal cases, the court may require witnesses to testify in court and may exclude statements that cannot be tested through cross-examination. In supervisory-transferred cases, witnesses may have given statements during the investigation and may not appear in court. The defendant may challenge the voluntariness of a confession, but the burden of proof may be difficult to discharge. To address this, the supervisory commission should produce complete and accurate records, including audio and video recordings of interrogations, and the procuratorate and court should have access to those records. The court should be able to summon investigators to explain the circumstances of the investigation when necessary. These measures would strengthen the credibility of the evidence and protect the defendant's right to a fair trial.

D. Liuzhi, Defense Rights, and Procedural Safeguards

The fourth controversy concerns liuzhi and defense rights. Liuzhi is a supervisory measure that restricts personal liberty. It is not criminal detention or arrest under the Criminal Procedure Law. During liuzhi, the person is not formally a criminal suspect, and defense counsel generally does not have the same access as in ordinary criminal proceedings. This has been criticized by some scholars and practitioners as creating a gap in procedural protection. The Supervision Law does provide safeguards, such as approval requirements, time limits, notification of family members, medical care, and supervision by higher-level supervisory organs. But these safeguards are not identical to those in the Criminal Procedure Law.

The justification for the distinction is that supervisory investigation is not criminal investigation and that the supervisory commission needs flexibility to investigate complex corruption cases. The counter-argument is that the seriousness of the coercive measure requires equivalent procedural protection, regardless of the label. A balanced approach would strengthen the safeguards without eliminating the distinction. For example, the law could require prompt notification of family members, access to medical care, regular review of the necessity of liuzhi, and audio-video recording of interrogations. After transfer to the procuratorate, the suspect should have full access to defense counsel, and the procuratorate should review the legality of the supervisory measures that produced the evidence. These measures would improve the legitimacy of the process without undermining the supervisory commission's independence.

E. Supervising the Supervisor

The fifth controversy concerns the supervision of the supervisory commission itself. The supervisory commission supervises all public officials, including officials in the procuratorate, the court, and the public security organ. But who supervises the supervisory commission? The Constitution and the Supervision Law provide for internal supervision, higher-level supervision, people's congress supervision, and Party supervision. The supervisory commission has internal disciplinary organs and procedures for handling misconduct by its own staff. The people's congress and its standing committee can hear reports and conduct inspections. The Party's discipline inspection system exercises political and disciplinary oversight. These mechanisms are important, but they are not the same as external legal supervision.

Some scholars have proposed that the procuratorate should have jurisdiction over duty-related crimes committed by supervisory commission staff. This would address the concern that the supervisory commission investigates its own personnel. Others argue that such a proposal would compromise the constitutional independence of the supervisory commission and create a conflict of interest because the procuratorate is itself subject to supervision. A more modest proposal is to strengthen internal review, create a separate disciplinary mechanism for supervisory staff, and enhance transparency through published guiding cases and annual reports. The goal is not to subject the supervisory commission to judicial control in the ordinary sense, but to ensure that its power is exercised lawfully and accountably.

F. Coordination and the Risk of Fragmentation

The sixth controversy concerns coordination. The anti-corruption system involves multiple organs: the supervisory commission, the procuratorate, the court, the public security organ, the audit organ, and the financial intelligence unit. Each has its own jurisdiction, procedures, and standards. Without effective coordination, cases can be delayed, evidence can be lost, and defendants can face inconsistent treatment. The Supervision Law provides for cooperation, but it does not establish a comprehensive coordination framework. Joint meetings and case-transfer rules are useful, but they are not a substitute for clear legal rules. A more systematic approach would include a national case-management platform, standardized evidence templates, joint training programs, and published guidance on jurisdictional boundaries. These measures would reduce fragmentation and improve the consistency of law implementation.

V. Conclusions and Recommendations

The Supervisory Commission is a constitutional innovation that has reshaped China's anti-corruption and supervision system. The Supervision Law grants supervisory commissions the powers of supervision, investigation, and disposition, and it establishes a constitutional relationship of cooperation and checking with judicial organs. The division of responsibilities is not a simple hierarchy. Supervisory commissions investigate duty-related crimes; procuratorates review cases for prosecution and exercise limited investigative jurisdiction over judicial staff misconduct; courts try cases and apply criminal procedure standards; public security organs investigate ordinary crimes and provide operational assistance. Each organ has its own constitutional function, and the system depends on mutual respect and effective coordination.

The analysis in this paper suggests that the current framework is workable but incomplete. The main gaps are jurisdictional ambiguity, evidentiary conversion, procedural safeguards during supervisory investigation, and external oversight of the supervisory commission. These gaps do not mean that the system is failing, but they do mean that further legal development is needed. The following recommendations are offered for improving law implementation.

First, clarify jurisdictional boundaries through authoritative interpretation. The Supervision Law and the Criminal Procedure Law should be read together to produce clear rules on the division between duty-related crimes and ordinary crimes, and between supervisory investigation and the procuratorate's residual jurisdiction over judicial staff misconduct. A primary-conduct test, supported by a formal dispute-resolution mechanism, would reduce uncertainty. Higher-level supervisory commissions and procuratorates should issue joint guidance on typical overlap scenarios.

Second, strengthen evidentiary standards and evidence conversion. Supervisory evidence should be held to the same standards of legality, authenticity, and voluntariness as criminal evidence. Interrogations should be recorded audio-visually, evidence chains should be documented, and the exclusionary rule should be applied consistently. The procuratorate should have access to the complete supervisory investigation record when reviewing a case, and the court should be able to examine the circumstances in which evidence was obtained. These measures would improve the credibility of prosecutions and protect defendants' rights.

Third, enhance procedural safeguards during supervisory investigation. Liuzhi should be subject to stricter approval, periodic review, and external monitoring. Family notification, medical care, and access to counsel after transfer should be guaranteed. The law should specify the consequences of procedural violations, including the exclusion of evidence obtained through serious violations. These safeguards would not undermine the supervisory commission's effectiveness; they would strengthen the legitimacy of its work.

Fourth, improve cooperation mechanisms. Supervisory commissions, procuratorates, courts, and public security organs should establish regular coordination meetings, joint training, and information-sharing protocols. Case-transfer procedures should be standardized, and asset recovery should be coordinated through a central mechanism. International cooperation should be strengthened through mutual legal assistance and extradition arrangements. These measures would reduce fragmentation and improve the efficiency of anti-corruption enforcement.

Fifth, strengthen oversight of the supervisory commission. Internal discipline, people's congress supervision, and Party supervision should be complemented by greater transparency. The supervisory commission should publish annual reports, guiding cases, and statistics on case handling. A separate mechanism for investigating misconduct by supervisory staff should be considered, with appropriate safeguards to preserve the commission's constitutional independence. The goal is to ensure that the supervisor is also supervised, without creating a conflict with the constitutional design.

Sixth, promote a trial-centered approach in supervisory-transferred cases. Courts should be able to examine evidence in open court, summon witnesses when necessary, and exclude illegally obtained evidence. The procuratorate should not treat supervisory investigation as a substitute for its own review. The court should not treat the transfer decision as a presumption of guilt. A genuine trial stage is essential to the legitimacy of the criminal process and to the credibility of the anti-corruption system.

In conclusion, the Supervisory Commission's authority scope under the National Supervision Law is broad but not unlimited. Its powers are constitutionally grounded, statutorily defined, and functionally distinct from judicial power. The division of responsibilities with judicial organs is based on cooperation and checking, not on hierarchy. The system has achieved significant results in anti-corruption, but it still faces challenges in jurisdictional clarity, procedural protection, evidentiary standards, and external oversight. Addressing these challenges through legal refinement, institutional coordination, and transparent practice will strengthen the rule of law and enhance public confidence in both the supervisory system and the judicial system.

Selected Sources

Constitution of the People's Republic of China, especially Articles 123 to 127 on supervisory commissions.

Supervision Law of the People's Republic of China, especially Articles 3, 4, 10, 11, 15, 22, 33, 34, and 45.

Criminal Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, especially Articles 19 and 170.

Criminal Law of the People's Republic of China, Chapters VIII and IX on corruption, bribery, abuse of power, and dereliction of duty.

Central Commission for Discipline Inspection and National Supervisory Commission, official publications and policy interpretations on supervisory investigation and case transfer.

Supreme People's Procuratorate and Supreme People's Court, guiding cases and work reports on duty-related crime prosecution and trial.

Academic literature on supervisory power, constitutional law, criminal procedure, and anti-corruption governance in China.
