chunkloop.response:
Basic Protagonist Setup

Rin Amamiya is sixteen years old and in her second year at Kanzaki Municipal High School, a squat concrete building at the edge of a town that seems to forget its own name after dark. She is the kind of girl who arrives twelve minutes early and sits where she can see the door. Teachers describe her as quiet, reliable, and a little too serious. Classmates describe her as the girl who always has a book, who never eats lunch in the cafeteria, who apologizes when someone else bumps into her. No one describes her as dangerous. That is the point. Rin has spent two years making herself small enough to be overlooked, and she has become very good at it.

Her personality is a careful arrangement of opposites. She is observant to the point of discomfort: she notices which shoe locker sticks, which teacher pauses before saying a student's name, which group of girls falls silent when she passes. She remembers rules with unusual precision, not because she loves authority, but because rules make the world feel briefly navigable. When she is anxious, she counts things. The four edges of a desk. The seven steps from the classroom door to her seat. The thirteen tiles in the corridor where the fluorescent light flickers. She has a dry, private sense of humor that she rarely lets anyone hear, and a temper that arrives so suddenly it frightens her. She wants to belong. She also tests people, quietly, to see when they will leave. Most of them do.

Rin is sensitive in the way a bruised nerve is sensitive. A sigh from her mother can ruin a week. A classmate's laughter behind her can turn into a sentence she hears for days. She is proud, too, which makes the loneliness worse. She will not ask to sit with anyone. She will not explain why she flinches when a hand lands on her shoulder. She has learned to smile at the right moments, and the smile looks almost real, which is why no one looks closer.

Since the winter of her first year of middle school, Rin has carried marks on her forearms that she hides under wristbands and long sleeves. She does not think of them as a cry for help. She thinks of them as a private language, a way to make an invisible hurt take up space. The habit began after a season she calls the gray winter: a close friend's secret was exposed, the class decided Rin was the one who had spoken, and the friend stopped looking at her. Rin, already raw from home, did not defend herself well. She shouted. She shoved a boy who mocked the friend. She was suspended for three days. When her mother was called to school, she listened to the vice principal, then looked at Rin with an exhaustion that was worse than anger. Why can't you just be easier, she said. The sentence did not sound cruel. That was what made it stay. Rin began to leave small, controlled hurts on her skin, not because she wanted to die, but because the larger pain had no shape and no witness. She knows now that this is a problem. She does not know how to ask for help without becoming the girl who needs help, and she is not ready to be that girl.

Her family life is polite and airless. She lives in a narrow apartment above a shuttered pharmacy with her mother, her stepfather, and her six-year-old half brother, Sota. Her biological father left when she was eleven, not with a fight but with a series of departures that grew longer and quieter. Now he sends postcards from cities he never names, with no return address and no question about her life. Rin keeps them in a tin box under her bed and tells herself she does not read them. Her mother works night shifts at the town hospital and loves Rin in a distracted, practical way: meals left in the refrigerator, notes about laundry, a hand on her forehead when she has a fever. Her stepfather, Daichi, is gentle and uncertain, the kind of man who knocks before entering a room he pays for. Sota adores Rin, and Rin is careful with him, as if affection is a cup she might spill. But she feels like a guest in her own home. The apartment has a new sofa, a new family photograph, a new routine, and Rin is the old furniture no one knows where to put.

At school, she has become an expert at being almost present. She is not bullied outright, which makes it harder to explain. She is simply not chosen. She eats alone in the library, volunteers for tasks no one wants, and keeps an apology notebook in which she writes sentences she never says aloud: I am sorry for being strange. I am sorry for making things awkward. I am sorry for existing at the wrong volume. She knows the notebook is a bad habit. She writes in it anyway. The only place she feels steady is in the old east annex, a building connected to the main school by a covered walkway. It is supposed to be off-limits after sunset, though no one explains why. Rin likes it because the clocks there run slow, the floorboards announce every footstep, and the silence feels honest. She has learned not to trust mirrors in that building. Sometimes her reflection seems a half-second late, and once, in the third-floor girls' bathroom, she saw a girl in a summer uniform standing behind her when the stalls were empty. She turned. No one was there. She told herself it was the light. She has told herself many things.

What makes Rin a dangerous person to follow into a suspense story is not that she is fearless. It is that she has already survived the worst thing she can imagine, which is being left, and she has survived it badly. She is brave for other people. If a younger student is crying in the stairwell, Rin will sit beside them even if she cannot find the right words. If a teacher humiliates a quiet boy, she will feel a hot, reckless anger rise in her chest. But she will not protect herself. She has decided, in some wordless part of her mind, that she deserves the consequences. This is the flaw that will lead her toward the school's hidden rules, the strange rumors, and the things that wait in the east annex. Rin does not go looking for ghosts. She goes looking for a rule that will finally tell her how to be forgiven. That is how the school finds her.

Core Storyline

Kanzaki Municipal High School's east annex is not simply haunted; it is governed. After the last bell, a laminated notice appears in the staff room and is removed before morning. Students call it the Evening Protocols. The rules are deceptively plain: do not enter the annex after six; never count the annex stairs aloud; if the corridor repeats a classroom door, do not turn around when someone calls your name; do not answer a voice that sounds like your own; keep your left hand on the wall until the exit sign appears; never run. Most students treat the list as a dare. Rin Amamiya treats it as evidence. She notices the annex clock loses seven minutes every evening and that the rules are written in two inks, as if amended by different hands. The annex smells of floor wax and wet plaster; its clocks tick at different speeds, and the corridor lights buzz like trapped flies. Her investigation begins when a first-year girl, Hina Mori, disappears between the second and third floors during cleaning duty. The school says Hina ran away. Rin finds Hina's shoe behind the stairwell door and, inside it, a folded note: Don't let them count you.

The first plotline, 'The Stair That Counts Back,' turns the Cursed Stairs into a puzzle of observation and memory. The annex staircase has thirteen steps. At 6:07 Rin counts fourteen; at 6:09 she counts twelve. The protocol forbids counting aloud, but Rin discovers a hidden condition: silent counting is permitted, and the staircase answers only a spoken number. When she whispers 'thirteen,' the step beneath her gives like wet cardboard, the lights fail, and a girl's voice above her says, 'You're late.' Rin breaks the rule on purpose to follow Hina's voice. The stairwell lengthens, each landing opening onto the same landing. The misleading legend says the stairs demand an apology; in truth they demand an exact count. The stairs are not evil; they are a rehearsal of blame. Each loop repeats a student's failure to be believed, and Rin recognizes the pattern because she has rehearsed her own apologies for years. To solve it, she must separate guilt from fact. Rin's habit of noticing small inconsistencies becomes her weapon. She learns that the loop preserves the moment a student was blamed for a prank and could not explain herself. To escape, Rin must speak the true number of steps without adding a plea or excuse. Her first attempt fails because she apologizes. Her second succeeds because she counts thirteen and steps down. Hina is alive on the landing but cannot remember her name. This plotline forces Rin's cognitive shift: she stops treating rules as moral commands and starts reading them as incomplete evidence.

The second plotline, 'The Corridor That Repeats,' makes the Endless Corridor the novel's central mystery of erased identity. Rin and a classmate test the rumor after a rainstorm. The protocol says never turn around in the east corridor. The hidden condition is that the corridor loops only when two people walk it in opposite directions, and the rule applies to whoever hears their name first. The notice is also misleading: one must turn at the third call, because the voice is copying the walker's own steps. The corridor tests her critical thinking: the rule is not a command but a set of conditions, and obedience without interpretation is fatal. Rin and her classmate are separated. Every door they pass is their homeroom, but the clock inside runs backward. Rin hears her mother's voice, then Hina's, then her own voice reciting the apologies she writes but never says. She almost turns on the first call. She waits, remembering the second ink. At the third call she turns toward the wall, not the voice, and the corridor folds open. She finds the old Adjustment Room, where difficult students were once 'counseled' and then quietly removed from the class register. The logbook lists Hina and, disturbingly, Rin herself, written years before she enrolled. This plotline raises the emotional stakes: Rin's private fear of being erased becomes a physical place. It also reveals the school's real antagonist, an administrative ritual rather than a ghost.

The third plotline, 'The Girl in the Third-Floor Mirror,' ties the stair and corridor to Rin's guilt. In the annex bathroom, Rin sees a girl in a summer uniform standing behind her, though the stalls are empty. The girl casts no reflection. The protocol warns against eye contact after sunset, but the hidden condition is that the mirror shows the person you are trying not to become. Rin breaks the taboo to save a younger student trapped in the bathroom overnight. The mirror girl is the residue of Emi Sato, a student bullied into silence after reporting a teacher. Emi's mother worked at the school and wrote the Evening Protocols, each rule a bandage over an institutional failure. The mirror also confronts Rin with her own hidden language of pain, the scars she conceals, and forces her to see self-erasure as another form of disappearance. Rin learns that stair, corridor, and mirror are three parts of one mechanism: the school's attempt to contain its own cruelty. To free Hina and the other lost students, Rin must gather the original rule sheet, the Adjustment Room log, and Emi's confession, then read them aloud in the east annex at 6:13, the minute the clock loses each day. The three plotlines converge because each has supplied one piece: the stair gives exactness, the corridor gives erased names, and the mirror gives the author's grief.

Rin's development is psychological as much as supernatural. She begins as a girl who obeys, apologizes, and shrinks; she becomes a girl who questions conditions, tests evidence, and accepts that rules can protect or wound. Her emotions do not become smaller—fear for Hina, anger at the Adjustment Room, grief for Emi remain intense—but she learns to act while feeling them. The suspense is whether she can break the final taboo without becoming another erased name.

Important Supporting Characters

The supporting cast of *The Evening Protocols* is designed to make the school feel populated and plausible before it becomes predatory. Each character grounds a different kind of pressure on Rin Amamiya: the pressure to protect, the pressure to remember, the pressure to trust an adult, and the pressure to look directly at what she has been avoiding. None of them is merely a helper or a victim. Each one is also a clue.

**Hina Mori** is the missing first-year student whose disappearance pulls Rin into the east annex. She is fourteen, small for her age, with a habit of collecting novelty erasers and laughing a half-second before anyone finishes a joke. Before she vanishes between the second and third floors during cleaning duty, she is the kind of girl teachers call “bright” because she is easy to manage: she volunteers, she writes neatly, she apologizes too often. Rin notices her because Hina eats lunch alone in the stairwell and pretends to be waiting for a friend. Their relationship begins as a small, unspoken recognition—two girls performing invisibility in different keys. When Rin finds Hina’s shoe behind the stairwell door, she also finds a folded note in the toe: *Don’t let them count you.* That note turns Rin from an observer into an investigator. After Rin retrieves her from the stair loop, Hina is alive but altered. She cannot remember her own name for three days. She follows Rin through the corridors like a younger sister, calling her “senpai,” then “Rin,” then sometimes a name that belongs to no one at Kanzaki High. Hina remembers fragments of the annex—wet plaster, a voice above the landing, the smell of floor wax—but not the order in which they happened. She is not a passive rescue object. She notices when adults lie, and she is the first to say that Mr. Sawada’s smile looks “like a door closing.” Her dependence forces Rin to act before she feels ready, and her damaged memory makes her a living piece of evidence: proof that the annex does not merely frighten students, it edits them.

**Aoi Kanzaki** is the novel’s possession-haunted character, inspired by old stories in which a grieving woman’s body is suddenly occupied by a dead mother’s voice. Aoi is Rin’s classmate and former friend: a practical, popular girl who serves as class representative and remembers everyone’s birthday. In their first year, Aoi once covered for Rin after a minor rule violation, and Rin—ashamed, suspicious of kindness—pushed her away. Their friendship cooled into polite distance. That guilt returns when Aoi volunteers to wait in the annex corridor while Rin retrieves Hina’s shoe. Afterward, Aoi begins to have episodes. At lunch she sits at a desk that has been out of use for years and writes left-handed in an old-fashioned script. She calls Mr. Sawada “Takeda-sensei,” a name no current student should know. She hums the school song from a graduation ceremony that took place before she was born. Most unsettling, she speaks in Emi Sato’s voice: soft, formal, and older than her body. When Aoi “returns,” she is terrified and ashamed, unable to explain where she has been. Her mother assumes exam stress; the school nurse gives her tea and a form. Rin recognizes the pattern from old possession anecdotes—the sudden shift in voice, the intimate knowledge of the dead, the way the body becomes a house for someone else’s grievance. But Aoi’s condition is tied directly to the annex: her episodes trigger at 6:07, when the clock loses seven minutes, and after she hears her own name called in the endless corridor. She is both a warning and a channel. Through Aoi’s mouth, Emi Sato reveals fragments of the Adjustment Room and the erased register. Rin’s relationship with Aoi is the story’s most painful bond because it mixes affection, guilt, and fear. To save Aoi, Rin may have to break the very rules that keep the corridor from swallowing them both.

**Mr. Kensuke Sawada** is the teacher figure who tries to intervene and fails because the problem is not the kind of problem his training can hold. He is in his late thirties, the homeroom teacher and counseling coordinator, a man with a tidy office and a sincere belief that problems can be solved through conversation, routine, and rational reframing. He notices Rin’s isolation, her scars, her apology notebook, her sudden absences. He uses the language of rational emotive therapy: identify the irrational belief, test it against evidence, replace it with a healthier thought. In another story, he might help her. Here, his kindness is real but insufficient. He asks Rin to stop spreading “rumor games.” He tells her that fear is a thought, not a place. He contacts her mother and recommends counseling. When Hina disappears, he enters the annex himself to prove that the corridor is ordinary. The building does not argue with him; it edits him. The corridor repeats his own counseling phrases back in his voice, then in Hina’s, then in a child’s voice he does not recognize. He emerges after what feels like ten minutes, though three hours have passed. His notebook is blank. He cannot remember Hina’s name, though he wrote her referral that morning. He remains kind, but he becomes unreliable in a way that isolates Rin further. His old guilt sharpens the tragedy: as a student teacher years ago, he signed a routine transfer form for a difficult girl named Emi Sato without reading the attached file. He does not remember her. The school remembers for him. His relationship with Rin is one of almost-trust—she wants to believe he can help, and his failure teaches her that adult rationality can be a locked door with a polite sign.

**Emi Sato**, the girl in the third-floor mirror, is the fourth key presence: less a living supporting character than a residue with a will. She was a second-year student who reported a teacher and was quietly erased from the class register; her mother, a former office clerk, wrote the Evening Protocols as a series of bandages over institutional failure. Emi appears in mirrors, in Aoi’s borrowed voice, and in the annex’s oldest photographs. She is not simply a villain. She is a witness who has been denied a name for so long that she tests everyone who enters her corridor. Her relationship with Rin is mirror-shaped: she shows Rin the person she is trying not to become, and she recognizes Rin’s private language of apology because she used a similar language herself. Emi’s voice is soft, formal, and dangerously reasonable. She asks Rin to count, to turn, to look—small requests that are also traps. To reach the climax, Rin must stop treating Emi as a ghost to escape and start treating her as a girl to name. Together, Hina, Aoi, Mr. Sawada, and Emi form the human architecture of the mystery: the child who must be protected, the friend who must be recovered, the adult who cannot see, and the erased girl who must finally be heard.

Specific Design of Surreal Elements

The surreal in The Evening Protocols is not decoration; it is the school's bureaucracy turned visible. The east annex is the pressure chamber. After the last bell, laminated rules appear in the staff room and vanish before morning. The annex clock loses seven minutes every evening, the corridor lights buzz like trapped flies, and the building smells of floor wax and wet plaster. The rules are written in two inks because they were amended: first by Emi Sato's mother, an office clerk trying to bandage institutional failures, then by the institution itself. The system has five parts—Cursed Stairs, Endless Corridor, Old School Building's Bathroom, Red Swimming Pool, and the Ghost in the Cooking Room—each with a visible rule, a hidden condition, a consequence, and a link to Rin Amamiya's private vocabulary of apology, self-erasure, and abandonment.

The Cursed Stairs are the annex staircase, which has thirteen nominal steps. At 6:07 it counts fourteen; at 6:09, twelve. The protocol forbids counting aloud, but the hidden condition is that silent counting is safe and only a spoken number makes the staircase answer. When Rin whispers 'thirteen,' the step gives like wet cardboard and a girl's voice above says, 'You're late.' The stairwell lengthens into repeated landings. Each loop preserves a moment when a student was blamed for something she could not explain. The stairs are not evil; they are a rehearsal of blame. Rin recognizes the pattern because she has spent years rehearsing apologies for existing, for the scars on her arms, for the trouble she believes she causes. To escape, she must speak the true number without adding a plea or excuse. Her first attempt fails because she apologizes; her second succeeds because she counts thirteen and steps down. Mechanically, the staircase is a memory loop keyed to an exact count. Thematically, it forces Rin to separate guilt from fact.

The Endless Corridor loops only when two people walk it in opposite directions; the rule applies to whoever hears her name first. The notice says never turn around. The hidden condition is that one must turn at the third call, toward the wall, because the voice is copying the walker's own steps. The corridor stretches, every door becomes the same homeroom, clocks run backward, and the voice cycles through her mother, Hina, and Rin's own apologies. At the third call she turns toward the wall and the corridor folds open onto the old Adjustment Room, where difficult students were counseled and quietly removed from the register. The logbook lists Hina and, impossibly, Rin years before she enrolled. The corridor is the novel's engine of erased identity: it makes Rin's fear of being abandoned into a place, then gives her evidence that the school has erased names before. It also shows why Aoi's possession matters—Aoi's borrowed voice is another corridor, another name spoken through a body.

In the Old School Building's Bathroom on the third floor of the annex, Rin sees a girl in a summer uniform behind her, though the stalls are empty. The girl casts no reflection. The protocol warns against eye contact after sunset; the hidden condition is that the mirror shows the person you are trying not to become. The bathroom is a threshold, not a trap: water in the sinks runs backward, stall doors open onto the same stall, and the mirror's surface warms like skin. Rin breaks the taboo to save a younger student locked inside overnight. The mirror girl is Emi Sato, the student erased after reporting a teacher. Emi is not simply a villain; she is a witness denied a name. For Rin, the mirror is the most intimate horror because it reflects the self-erasure she has practiced with a blade and a sleeve. The scars are her hidden writing, and the mirror reads them as another form of disappearance. To leave, Rin must look directly at Emi and say her name, not her own apology.

The Red Swimming Pool is ordinary until sunset, when the lane ropes bleed red and the water holds reflections a half-second late. The posted rule says do not swim when the ropes are red. The hidden condition is that the pool is not dragging swimmers under; it is showing the weight of a name the school tried to wash out. A hand closes around a lone swimmer's ankle, but it loosens only when the swimmer speaks the erased student's name and exits without looking back. The red is rust, iron, and old disinfectant from the drainage channel beneath the annex, but it is also the color Rin associates with her own scars and with the relief she once sought in pain. The pool therefore externalizes her impulse to hurt herself in order to feel real. At the climax, its red surface reflects the missing line from the Adjustment Room log, giving Rin the final name she needs. The pool's mechanic is reflection plus release: the school's history must be named, not scrubbed away.

The Ghost in the Cooking Room is a woman in a faded apron who stirs an empty pot at dusk and asks, 'Have you eaten?' She is not very frightening; she is sad. The rule says answer politely and leave before the timer rings. The hidden condition is that she responds to honesty, not manners. If a student lies, the room fills with steam and the exit hides; if a student answers truthfully, she points to the old service hatch that leads to the Adjustment Room's back corridor. She is the residue of a former home-economics teacher, Ms. Takeda, who kept a private ledger of students who ate alone and who remembered Emi when the register did not. Her ledger supplies one erased name. For Rin, the cooking-room ghost is a gentle accusation: Rin skips meals, hides hunger, and treats self-neglect as discipline. The ghost sees the caretaking Rin refuses to ask for.

These phenomena are one mechanism, not five separate rumors. The school's history of removing difficult students has made its rules literal; the surreal is the institution's cruelty continuing as architecture. Each element also matches Rin's psychology: stairs rehearse blame, corridor repeats abandonment, mirror exposes self-erasure, pool reddens like old wounds, cooking room names neglect. The rules are incomplete evidence, and the hidden conditions force Rin to interpret rather than obey. At 6:13, the minute the annex clock loses each day, she must gather the original rule sheet, the Adjustment Room log, and Emi's confession and read them aloud. The stairs give exactness, the corridor gives erased names, the bathroom gives the author's grief, the pool gives reflection, and the cooking room gives the name that was almost forgotten. The climax works only because the surreal has been tied to plot and character: Rin cannot defeat the annex by running; she must count, turn, look, name, and eat—small human acts that the school tried to make impossible.

**Climax and Ending of the Story**

By 5:58 the east annex was empty in the way a held breath is empty. Rin Amamiya stood at the foot of the staircase with her blazer buttoned wrong and three documents folded against her ribs: the original rule sheet, the Adjustment Room log, and the single page torn from Ms. Takeda's ledger. At 6:06 the annex clock would hand back its seven stolen minutes, and at 6:13 those minutes would be spent. Anyone still inside when the hands closed the gap would simply stop being listed — no body, no obituary, only a class register that no longer agreed with anyone's memory. That was the death the annex offered. It was tidier than a blade and far more complete.

Aoi was on the third floor. Rin had watched her go up at 5:40, walking with her head tilted as though listening to someone a half-step behind her, and she had not come down. The bathroom door stood open. Inside, the sinks were running backward, water climbing the porcelain in thin clear ropes, and the mirror had gone warm the way a forehead goes warm before a fever breaks. Aoi stood at the basin with both hands flat on the rim. Her reflection faced her. Behind her reflection, there was a second girl in a summer uniform, and that girl had no reflection at all.

"You're late," Aoi said, and it was not Aoi's voice. It was younger, flatter, with the accent of someone who had learned to speak quietly in offices. "You're late, and you're going to apologize. Everyone apologizes. Nobody ever says the thing."

Rin's first instinct was the old one, the one her mother's voice had planted years ago: take the blame, absorb it, keep the room calm. Her scars prickled under her sleeve like writing trying to be read. She made herself look at the mirror instead. In it, the second girl's mouth was moving a moment before Aoi's did, and Aoi's lips were going grey at the edges, her pulse jumping thin and fast under the jaw. Behind them, water had begun to seep from the corridor, red as the lane ropes at sunset, red as rust, red as the relief Rin had once chased with a blade.

She had perhaps ninety seconds of choice, and the choice was genuinely a knife's edge. If she grabbed Aoi and ran, the corridor would loop — she could already hear it starting, doors becoming the same door — and two names would go missing instead of one. If she stayed and did the work, and did it wrong, Aoi's heart would keep the annex's time forever.

So Rin did not argue and did not run. She did what the elders in her grandmother's village story had done when the dead woman stood up in the aunt's body and accused the living: she stopped defending herself, named the dead, and listened.

She took the stairs first. Thirteen nominal steps, fourteen at 6:07, twelve at 6:09. The protocol forbade counting aloud; the hidden condition was that silence was safe and only a spoken number made the staircase answer. On her first attempt she whispered, "Thirteen — I'm sorry, I'm sorry, I know I'm in the way," and the step gave under her like wet cardboard and dropped her into a landing she had already climbed. The second time she said only, "Thirteen," and stepped down. The stairwell exhaled.

At the corridor she heard her name called three times: once in her mother's voice, once in Hina's, once in her own. She walked on past the first two and turned at the third — not around, but toward the wall, because the voice was only copying her footsteps — and the corridor folded open onto the Adjustment Room, dust, a wall of hooks, and the logbook where Hina's name was written in 2019 and, in a hand forty years older, her own.

At 6:12 she stood back in the bathroom with the three documents and read them aloud. The rule sheet in two inks. The log's dates and student numbers. The ledger page where a home-economics teacher had written, in pencil, the name the register had swallowed: *Sato, Emi. Third year. Reported a teacher in March. Withdrawn in April, no forwarding address, no exam record.*

"Emi Sato," Rin said, to the mirror, to the grey-lipped girl, to the reflection that was not a reflection. "You reported him and they took your name instead. That was done to you. It was not your fault, and it was not a punishment you earned."

Aoi's body convulsed. Water slapped the tiles. From the corridor came the cooking-room timer, thin as a teaspoon on a saucer, and Rin did the last thing: she walked to the service hatch, answered the aproned woman honestly when asked whether she had eaten, and ate the rice put in front of her, cold, in three swallows, while the steam banked and thinned. "She remembers me," the ghost said, and pointed.

Then the promise — not the grand one, the keepable one. Rin did not swear to fix the school. She swore to have Emi's name read at assembly, to keep her desk unissued for the term, and to say the name aloud once a week until she graduated. The elders had promised the dead mother only that the child would not be hit again. That was enough. It had always been enough.

At 6:13 Aoi fell. The red water went out of the corridor like a plug pulled, the mirror cooled, and the clock ticked the minute it had been owed. Aoi sat up on the tiles, blinked at the running taps, and asked, bewildered, "Why am I here? What are you all doing?" She remembers none of it. She never will. She remembers only that Rin, for reasons she cannot explain, will not let go of her sleeve.

The cause was ordinary and unbearable. Emi Sato told a teacher's story to the wrong adult, and the school, which had been quietly removing inconvenient students since the annex was built, removed her the cheapest way available — by paperwork. Her mother worked the office and wrote the first protocols to contain what the building had become; the building amended them. The ghost was never a monster. She was a grievance with a filing system, and possession was simply the only mouth she had left.

A month later the assembly read a name that appeared on no register. Aoi and Rin eat lunch on the roof now, badly and often. In September a new laminated sheet appears in the staff room, and in a handwriting no one on staff recognizes, a clause has been added beneath the old ones — and on the first evening of term, a first-year girl in the annex corridor hears her name called once, twice, and then a third time, and turns toward the wall.

adaptive.response:
Basic Protagonist Setup

Rin Amamiya is sixteen years old and in her second year at Kanzaki Municipal High School, a squat concrete building at the edge of a town that seems to forget its own name after dark. She is the kind of girl who arrives twelve minutes early and sits where she can see the door. Teachers describe her as quiet, reliable, and a little too serious. Classmates describe her as the girl who always has a book, who never eats lunch in the cafeteria, who apologizes when someone else bumps into her. No one describes her as dangerous. That is the point. Rin has spent two years making herself small enough to be overlooked, and she has become very good at it.

Her personality is a careful arrangement of opposites. She is observant to the point of discomfort: she notices which shoe locker sticks, which teacher pauses before saying a student's name, which group of girls falls silent when she passes. She remembers rules with unusual precision, not because she loves authority, but because rules make the world feel briefly navigable. When she is anxious, she counts things. The four edges of a desk. The seven steps from the classroom door to her seat. The thirteen tiles in the corridor where the fluorescent light flickers. She has a dry, private sense of humor that she rarely lets anyone hear, and a temper that arrives so suddenly it frightens her. She wants to belong. She also tests people, quietly, to see when they will leave. Most of them do.

Rin is sensitive in the way a bruised nerve is sensitive. A sigh from her mother can ruin a week. A classmate's laughter behind her can turn into a sentence she hears for days. She is proud, too, which makes the loneliness worse. She will not ask to sit with anyone. She will not explain why she flinches when a hand lands on her shoulder. She has learned to smile at the right moments, and the smile looks almost real, which is why no one looks closer.

Since the winter of her first year of middle school, Rin has carried marks on her forearms that she hides under wristbands and long sleeves. She does not think of them as a cry for help. She thinks of them as a private language, a way to make an invisible hurt take up space. The habit began after a season she calls the gray winter: a close friend's secret was exposed, the class decided Rin was the one who had spoken, and the friend stopped looking at her. Rin, already raw from home, did not defend herself well. She shouted. She shoved a boy who mocked the friend. She was suspended for three days. When her mother was called to school, she listened to the vice principal, then looked at Rin with an exhaustion that was worse than anger. Why can't you just be easier, she said. The sentence did not sound cruel. That was what made it stay. Rin began to leave small, controlled hurts on her skin, not because she wanted to die, but because the larger pain had no shape and no witness. She knows now that this is a problem. She does not know how to ask for help without becoming the girl who needs help, and she is not ready to be that girl.

Her family life is polite and airless. She lives in a narrow apartment above a shuttered pharmacy with her mother, her stepfather, and her six-year-old half brother, Sota. Her biological father left when she was eleven, not with a fight but with a series of departures that grew longer and quieter. Now he sends postcards from cities he never names, with no return address and no question about her life. Rin keeps them in a tin box under her bed and tells herself she does not read them. Her mother works night shifts at the town hospital and loves Rin in a distracted, practical way: meals left in the refrigerator, notes about laundry, a hand on her forehead when she has a fever. Her stepfather, Daichi, is gentle and uncertain, the kind of man who knocks before entering a room he pays for. Sota adores Rin, and Rin is careful with him, as if affection is a cup she might spill. But she feels like a guest in her own home. The apartment has a new sofa, a new family photograph, a new routine, and Rin is the old furniture no one knows where to put.

At school, she has become an expert at being almost present. She is not bullied outright, which makes it harder to explain. She is simply not chosen. She eats alone in the library, volunteers for tasks no one wants, and keeps an apology notebook in which she writes sentences she never says aloud: I am sorry for being strange. I am sorry for making things awkward. I am sorry for existing at the wrong volume. She knows the notebook is a bad habit. She writes in it anyway. The only place she feels steady is in the old east annex, a building connected to the main school by a covered walkway. It is supposed to be off-limits after sunset, though no one explains why. Rin likes it because the clocks there run slow, the floorboards announce every footstep, and the silence feels honest. She has learned not to trust mirrors in that building. Sometimes her reflection seems a half-second late, and once, in the third-floor girls' bathroom, she saw a girl in a summer uniform standing behind her when the stalls were empty. She turned. No one was there. She told herself it was the light. She has told herself many things.

What makes Rin a dangerous person to follow into a suspense story is not that she is fearless. It is that she has already survived the worst thing she can imagine, which is being left, and she has survived it badly. She is brave for other people. If a younger student is crying in the stairwell, Rin will sit beside them even if she cannot find the right words. If a teacher humiliates a quiet boy, she will feel a hot, reckless anger rise in her chest. But she will not protect herself. She has decided, in some wordless part of her mind, that she deserves the consequences. This is the flaw that will lead her toward the school's hidden rules, the strange rumors, and the things that wait in the east annex. Rin does not go looking for ghosts. She goes looking for a rule that will finally tell her how to be forgiven. That is how the school finds her.

Core Storyline

Kanzaki Municipal High School's east annex is not simply haunted; it is governed. After the last bell, a laminated notice appears in the staff room and is removed before morning. Students call it the Evening Protocols. The rules are deceptively plain: do not enter the annex after six; never count the annex stairs aloud; if the corridor repeats a classroom door, do not turn around when someone calls your name; do not answer a voice that sounds like your own; keep your left hand on the wall until the exit sign appears; never run. Most students treat the list as a dare. Rin Amamiya treats it as evidence. She notices the annex clock loses seven minutes every evening and that the rules are written in two inks, as if amended by different hands. The annex smells of floor wax and wet plaster; its clocks tick at different speeds, and the corridor lights buzz like trapped flies. Her investigation begins when a first-year girl, Hina Mori, disappears between the second and third floors during cleaning duty. The school says Hina ran away. Rin finds Hina's shoe behind the stairwell door and, inside it, a folded note: Don't let them count you.

The first plotline, 'The Stair That Counts Back,' turns the Cursed Stairs into a puzzle of observation and memory. The annex staircase has thirteen steps. At 6:07 Rin counts fourteen; at 6:09 she counts twelve. The protocol forbids counting aloud, but Rin discovers a hidden condition: silent counting is permitted, and the staircase answers only a spoken number. When she whispers 'thirteen,' the step beneath her gives like wet cardboard, the lights fail, and a girl's voice above her says, 'You're late.' Rin breaks the rule on purpose to follow Hina's voice. The stairwell lengthens, each landing opening onto the same landing. The misleading legend says the stairs demand an apology; in truth they demand an exact count. The stairs are not evil; they are a rehearsal of blame. Each loop repeats a student's failure to be believed, and Rin recognizes the pattern because she has rehearsed her own apologies for years. To solve it, she must separate guilt from fact. Rin's habit of noticing small inconsistencies becomes her weapon. She learns that the loop preserves the moment a student was blamed for a prank and could not explain herself. To escape, Rin must speak the true number of steps without adding a plea or excuse. Her first attempt fails because she apologizes. Her second succeeds because she counts thirteen and steps down. Hina is alive on the landing but cannot remember her name. This plotline forces Rin's cognitive shift: she stops treating rules as moral commands and starts reading them as incomplete evidence.

The second plotline, 'The Corridor That Repeats,' makes the Endless Corridor the novel's central mystery of erased identity. Rin and a classmate test the rumor after a rainstorm. The protocol says never turn around in the east corridor. The hidden condition is that the corridor loops only when two people walk it in opposite directions, and the rule applies to whoever hears their name first. The notice is also misleading: one must turn at the third call, because the voice is copying the walker's own steps. The corridor tests her critical thinking: the rule is not a command but a set of conditions, and obedience without interpretation is fatal. Rin and her classmate are separated. Every door they pass is their homeroom, but the clock inside runs backward. Rin hears her mother's voice, then Hina's, then her own voice reciting the apologies she writes but never says. She almost turns on the first call. She waits, remembering the second ink. At the third call she turns toward the wall, not the voice, and the corridor folds open. She finds the old Adjustment Room, where difficult students were once 'counseled' and then quietly removed from the class register. The logbook lists Hina and, disturbingly, Rin herself, written years before she enrolled. This plotline raises the emotional stakes: Rin's private fear of being erased becomes a physical place. It also reveals the school's real antagonist, an administrative ritual rather than a ghost.

The third plotline, 'The Girl in the Third-Floor Mirror,' ties the stair and corridor to Rin's guilt. In the annex bathroom, Rin sees a girl in a summer uniform standing behind her, though the stalls are empty. The girl casts no reflection. The protocol warns against eye contact after sunset, but the hidden condition is that the mirror shows the person you are trying not to become. Rin breaks the taboo to save a younger student trapped in the bathroom overnight. The mirror girl is the residue of Emi Sato, a student bullied into silence after reporting a teacher. Emi's mother worked at the school and wrote the Evening Protocols, each rule a bandage over an institutional failure. The mirror also confronts Rin with her own hidden language of pain, the scars she conceals, and forces her to see self-erasure as another form of disappearance. Rin learns that stair, corridor, and mirror are three parts of one mechanism: the school's attempt to contain its own cruelty. To free Hina and the other lost students, Rin must gather the original rule sheet, the Adjustment Room log, and Emi's confession, then read them aloud in the east annex at 6:13, the minute the clock loses each day. The three plotlines converge because each has supplied one piece: the stair gives exactness, the corridor gives erased names, and the mirror gives the author's grief.

Rin's development is psychological as much as supernatural. She begins as a girl who obeys, apologizes, and shrinks; she becomes a girl who questions conditions, tests evidence, and accepts that rules can protect or wound. Her emotions do not become smaller—fear for Hina, anger at the Adjustment Room, grief for Emi remain intense—but she learns to act while feeling them. The suspense is whether she can break the final taboo without becoming another erased name.

Important Supporting Characters

The supporting cast of *The Evening Protocols* is designed to make the school feel populated and plausible before it becomes predatory. Each character grounds a different kind of pressure on Rin Amamiya: the pressure to protect, the pressure to remember, the pressure to trust an adult, and the pressure to look directly at what she has been avoiding. None of them is merely a helper or a victim. Each one is also a clue.

**Hina Mori** is the missing first-year student whose disappearance pulls Rin into the east annex. She is fourteen, small for her age, with a habit of collecting novelty erasers and laughing a half-second before anyone finishes a joke. Before she vanishes between the second and third floors during cleaning duty, she is the kind of girl teachers call “bright” because she is easy to manage: she volunteers, she writes neatly, she apologizes too often. Rin notices her because Hina eats lunch alone in the stairwell and pretends to be waiting for a friend. Their relationship begins as a small, unspoken recognition—two girls performing invisibility in different keys. When Rin finds Hina’s shoe behind the stairwell door, she also finds a folded note in the toe: *Don’t let them count you.* That note turns Rin from an observer into an investigator. After Rin retrieves her from the stair loop, Hina is alive but altered. She cannot remember her own name for three days. She follows Rin through the corridors like a younger sister, calling her “senpai,” then “Rin,” then sometimes a name that belongs to no one at Kanzaki High. Hina remembers fragments of the annex—wet plaster, a voice above the landing, the smell of floor wax—but not the order in which they happened. She is not a passive rescue object. She notices when adults lie, and she is the first to say that Mr. Sawada’s smile looks “like a door closing.” Her dependence forces Rin to act before she feels ready, and her damaged memory makes her a living piece of evidence: proof that the annex does not merely frighten students, it edits them.

**Aoi Kanzaki** is the novel’s possession-haunted character, inspired by old stories in which a grieving woman’s body is suddenly occupied by a dead mother’s voice. Aoi is Rin’s classmate and former friend: a practical, popular girl who serves as class representative and remembers everyone’s birthday. In their first year, Aoi once covered for Rin after a minor rule violation, and Rin—ashamed, suspicious of kindness—pushed her away. Their friendship cooled into polite distance. That guilt returns when Aoi volunteers to wait in the annex corridor while Rin retrieves Hina’s shoe. Afterward, Aoi begins to have episodes. At lunch she sits at a desk that has been out of use for years and writes left-handed in an old-fashioned script. She calls Mr. Sawada “Takeda-sensei,” a name no current student should know. She hums the school song from a graduation ceremony that took place before she was born. Most unsettling, she speaks in Emi Sato’s voice: soft, formal, and older than her body. When Aoi “returns,” she is terrified and ashamed, unable to explain where she has been. Her mother assumes exam stress; the school nurse gives her tea and a form. Rin recognizes the pattern from old possession anecdotes—the sudden shift in voice, the intimate knowledge of the dead, the way the body becomes a house for someone else’s grievance. But Aoi’s condition is tied directly to the annex: her episodes trigger at 6:07, when the clock loses seven minutes, and after she hears her own name called in the endless corridor. She is both a warning and a channel. Through Aoi’s mouth, Emi Sato reveals fragments of the Adjustment Room and the erased register. Rin’s relationship with Aoi is the story’s most painful bond because it mixes affection, guilt, and fear. To save Aoi, Rin may have to break the very rules that keep the corridor from swallowing them both.

**Mr. Kensuke Sawada** is the teacher figure who tries to intervene and fails because the problem is not the kind of problem his training can hold. He is in his late thirties, the homeroom teacher and counseling coordinator, a man with a tidy office and a sincere belief that problems can be solved through conversation, routine, and rational reframing. He notices Rin’s isolation, her scars, her apology notebook, her sudden absences. He uses the language of rational emotive therapy: identify the irrational belief, test it against evidence, replace it with a healthier thought. In another story, he might help her. Here, his kindness is real but insufficient. He asks Rin to stop spreading “rumor games.” He tells her that fear is a thought, not a place. He contacts her mother and recommends counseling. When Hina disappears, he enters the annex himself to prove that the corridor is ordinary. The building does not argue with him; it edits him. The corridor repeats his own counseling phrases back in his voice, then in Hina’s, then in a child’s voice he does not recognize. He emerges after what feels like ten minutes, though three hours have passed. His notebook is blank. He cannot remember Hina’s name, though he wrote her referral that morning. He remains kind, but he becomes unreliable in a way that isolates Rin further. His old guilt sharpens the tragedy: as a student teacher years ago, he signed a routine transfer form for a difficult girl named Emi Sato without reading the attached file. He does not remember her. The school remembers for him. His relationship with Rin is one of almost-trust—she wants to believe he can help, and his failure teaches her that adult rationality can be a locked door with a polite sign.

**Emi Sato**, the girl in the third-floor mirror, is the fourth key presence: less a living supporting character than a residue with a will. She was a second-year student who reported a teacher and was quietly erased from the class register; her mother, a former office clerk, wrote the Evening Protocols as a series of bandages over institutional failure. Emi appears in mirrors, in Aoi’s borrowed voice, and in the annex’s oldest photographs. She is not simply a villain. She is a witness who has been denied a name for so long that she tests everyone who enters her corridor. Her relationship with Rin is mirror-shaped: she shows Rin the person she is trying not to become, and she recognizes Rin’s private language of apology because she used a similar language herself. Emi’s voice is soft, formal, and dangerously reasonable. She asks Rin to count, to turn, to look—small requests that are also traps. To reach the climax, Rin must stop treating Emi as a ghost to escape and start treating her as a girl to name. Together, Hina, Aoi, Mr. Sawada, and Emi form the human architecture of the mystery: the child who must be protected, the friend who must be recovered, the adult who cannot see, and the erased girl who must finally be heard.

Specific Design of Surreal Elements

The surreal in The Evening Protocols is not decoration; it is the school's bureaucracy turned visible. The east annex is the pressure chamber. After the last bell, laminated rules appear in the staff room and vanish before morning. The annex clock loses seven minutes every evening, the corridor lights buzz like trapped flies, and the building smells of floor wax and wet plaster. The rules are written in two inks because they were amended: first by Emi Sato's mother, an office clerk trying to bandage institutional failures, then by the institution itself. The system has five parts—Cursed Stairs, Endless Corridor, Old School Building's Bathroom, Red Swimming Pool, and the Ghost in the Cooking Room—each with a visible rule, a hidden condition, a consequence, and a link to Rin Amamiya's private vocabulary of apology, self-erasure, and abandonment.

The Cursed Stairs are the annex staircase, which has thirteen nominal steps. At 6:07 it counts fourteen; at 6:09, twelve. The protocol forbids counting aloud, but the hidden condition is that silent counting is safe and only a spoken number makes the staircase answer. When Rin whispers 'thirteen,' the step gives like wet cardboard and a girl's voice above says, 'You're late.' The stairwell lengthens into repeated landings. Each loop preserves a moment when a student was blamed for something she could not explain. The stairs are not evil; they are a rehearsal of blame. Rin recognizes the pattern because she has spent years rehearsing apologies for existing, for the scars on her arms, for the trouble she believes she causes. To escape, she must speak the true number without adding a plea or excuse. Her first attempt fails because she apologizes; her second succeeds because she counts thirteen and steps down. Mechanically, the staircase is a memory loop keyed to an exact count. Thematically, it forces Rin to separate guilt from fact.

The Endless Corridor loops only when two people walk it in opposite directions; the rule applies to whoever hears her name first. The notice says never turn around. The hidden condition is that one must turn at the third call, toward the wall, because the voice is copying the walker's own steps. The corridor stretches, every door becomes the same homeroom, clocks run backward, and the voice cycles through her mother, Hina, and Rin's own apologies. At the third call she turns toward the wall and the corridor folds open onto the old Adjustment Room, where difficult students were counseled and quietly removed from the register. The logbook lists Hina and, impossibly, Rin years before she enrolled. The corridor is the novel's engine of erased identity: it makes Rin's fear of being abandoned into a place, then gives her evidence that the school has erased names before. It also shows why Aoi's possession matters—Aoi's borrowed voice is another corridor, another name spoken through a body.

In the Old School Building's Bathroom on the third floor of the annex, Rin sees a girl in a summer uniform behind her, though the stalls are empty. The girl casts no reflection. The protocol warns against eye contact after sunset; the hidden condition is that the mirror shows the person you are trying not to become. The bathroom is a threshold, not a trap: water in the sinks runs backward, stall doors open onto the same stall, and the mirror's surface warms like skin. Rin breaks the taboo to save a younger student locked inside overnight. The mirror girl is Emi Sato, the student erased after reporting a teacher. Emi is not simply a villain; she is a witness denied a name. For Rin, the mirror is the most intimate horror because it reflects the self-erasure she has practiced with a blade and a sleeve. The scars are her hidden writing, and the mirror reads them as another form of disappearance. To leave, Rin must look directly at Emi and say her name, not her own apology.

The Red Swimming Pool is ordinary until sunset, when the lane ropes bleed red and the water holds reflections a half-second late. The posted rule says do not swim when the ropes are red. The hidden condition is that the pool is not dragging swimmers under; it is showing the weight of a name the school tried to wash out. A hand closes around a lone swimmer's ankle, but it loosens only when the swimmer speaks the erased student's name and exits without looking back. The red is rust, iron, and old disinfectant from the drainage channel beneath the annex, but it is also the color Rin associates with her own scars and with the relief she once sought in pain. The pool therefore externalizes her impulse to hurt herself in order to feel real. At the climax, its red surface reflects the missing line from the Adjustment Room log, giving Rin the final name she needs. The pool's mechanic is reflection plus release: the school's history must be named, not scrubbed away.

The Ghost in the Cooking Room is a woman in a faded apron who stirs an empty pot at dusk and asks, 'Have you eaten?' She is not very frightening; she is sad. The rule says answer politely and leave before the timer rings. The hidden condition is that she responds to honesty, not manners. If a student lies, the room fills with steam and the exit hides; if a student answers truthfully, she points to the old service hatch that leads to the Adjustment Room's back corridor. She is the residue of a former home-economics teacher, Ms. Takeda, who kept a private ledger of students who ate alone and who remembered Emi when the register did not. Her ledger supplies one erased name. For Rin, the cooking-room ghost is a gentle accusation: Rin skips meals, hides hunger, and treats self-neglect as discipline. The ghost sees the caretaking Rin refuses to ask for.

These phenomena are one mechanism, not five separate rumors. The school's history of removing difficult students has made its rules literal; the surreal is the institution's cruelty continuing as architecture. Each element also matches Rin's psychology: stairs rehearse blame, corridor repeats abandonment, mirror exposes self-erasure, pool reddens like old wounds, cooking room names neglect. The rules are incomplete evidence, and the hidden conditions force Rin to interpret rather than obey. At 6:13, the minute the annex clock loses each day, she must gather the original rule sheet, the Adjustment Room log, and Emi's confession and read them aloud. The stairs give exactness, the corridor gives erased names, the bathroom gives the author's grief, the pool gives reflection, and the cooking room gives the name that was almost forgotten. The climax works only because the surreal has been tied to plot and character: Rin cannot defeat the annex by running; she must count, turn, look, name, and eat—small human acts that the school tried to make impossible.

**Climax and Ending of the Story**

By 5:58 the east annex was empty in the way a held breath is empty. Rin Amamiya stood at the foot of the staircase with her blazer buttoned wrong and three documents folded against her ribs: the original rule sheet, the Adjustment Room log, and the single page torn from Ms. Takeda's ledger. At 6:06 the annex clock would hand back its seven stolen minutes, and at 6:13 those minutes would be spent. Anyone still inside when the hands closed the gap would simply stop being listed — no body, no obituary, only a class register that no longer agreed with anyone's memory. That was the death the annex offered. It was tidier than a blade and far more complete.

Aoi was on the third floor. Rin had watched her go up at 5:40, walking with her head tilted as though listening to someone a half-step behind her, and she had not come down. The bathroom door stood open. Inside, the sinks were running backward, water climbing the porcelain in thin clear ropes, and the mirror had gone warm the way a forehead goes warm before a fever breaks. Aoi stood at the basin with both hands flat on the rim. Her reflection faced her. Behind her reflection, there was a second girl in a summer uniform, and that girl had no reflection at all.

"You're late," Aoi said, and it was not Aoi's voice. It was younger, flatter, with the accent of someone who had learned to speak quietly in offices. "You're late, and you're going to apologize. Everyone apologizes. Nobody ever says the thing."

Rin's first instinct was the old one, the one her mother's voice had planted years ago: take the blame, absorb it, keep the room calm. Her scars prickled under her sleeve like writing trying to be read. She made herself look at the mirror instead. In it, the second girl's mouth was moving a moment before Aoi's did, and Aoi's lips were going grey at the edges, her pulse jumping thin and fast under the jaw. Behind them, water had begun to seep from the corridor, red as the lane ropes at sunset, red as rust, red as the relief Rin had once chased with a blade.

She had perhaps ninety seconds of choice, and the choice was genuinely a knife's edge. If she grabbed Aoi and ran, the corridor would loop — she could already hear it starting, doors becoming the same door — and two names would go missing instead of one. If she stayed and did the work, and did it wrong, Aoi's heart would keep the annex's time forever.

So Rin did not argue and did not run. She did what the elders in her grandmother's village story had done when the dead woman stood up in the aunt's body and accused the living: she stopped defending herself, named the dead, and listened.

She took the stairs first. Thirteen nominal steps, fourteen at 6:07, twelve at 6:09. The protocol forbade counting aloud; the hidden condition was that silence was safe and only a spoken number made the staircase answer. On her first attempt she whispered, "Thirteen — I'm sorry, I'm sorry, I know I'm in the way," and the step gave under her like wet cardboard and dropped her into a landing she had already climbed. The second time she said only, "Thirteen," and stepped down. The stairwell exhaled.

At the corridor she heard her name called three times: once in her mother's voice, once in Hina's, once in her own. She walked on past the first two and turned at the third — not around, but toward the wall, because the voice was only copying her footsteps — and the corridor folded open onto the Adjustment Room, dust, a wall of hooks, and the logbook where Hina's name was written in 2019 and, in a hand forty years older, her own.

At 6:12 she stood back in the bathroom with the three documents and read them aloud. The rule sheet in two inks. The log's dates and student numbers. The ledger page where a home-economics teacher had written, in pencil, the name the register had swallowed: *Sato, Emi. Third year. Reported a teacher in March. Withdrawn in April, no forwarding address, no exam record.*

"Emi Sato," Rin said, to the mirror, to the grey-lipped girl, to the reflection that was not a reflection. "You reported him and they took your name instead. That was done to you. It was not your fault, and it was not a punishment you earned."

Aoi's body convulsed. Water slapped the tiles. From the corridor came the cooking-room timer, thin as a teaspoon on a saucer, and Rin did the last thing: she walked to the service hatch, answered the aproned woman honestly when asked whether she had eaten, and ate the rice put in front of her, cold, in three swallows, while the steam banked and thinned. "She remembers me," the ghost said, and pointed.

Then the promise — not the grand one, the keepable one. Rin did not swear to fix the school. She swore to have Emi's name read at assembly, to keep her desk unissued for the term, and to say the name aloud once a week until she graduated. The elders had promised the dead mother only that the child would not be hit again. That was enough. It had always been enough.

At 6:13 Aoi fell. The red water went out of the corridor like a plug pulled, the mirror cooled, and the clock ticked the minute it had been owed. Aoi sat up on the tiles, blinked at the running taps, and asked, bewildered, "Why am I here? What are you all doing?" She remembers none of it. She never will. She remembers only that Rin, for reasons she cannot explain, will not let go of her sleeve.

The cause was ordinary and unbearable. Emi Sato told a teacher's story to the wrong adult, and the school, which had been quietly removing inconvenient students since the annex was built, removed her the cheapest way available — by paperwork. Her mother worked the office and wrote the first protocols to contain what the building had become; the building amended them. The ghost was never a monster. She was a grievance with a filing system, and possession was simply the only mouth she had left.

A month later the assembly read a name that appeared on no register. Aoi and Rin eat lunch on the roof now, badly and often. In September a new laminated sheet appears in the staff room, and in a handwriting no one on staff recognizes, a clause has been added beneath the old ones — and on the first evening of term, a first-year girl in the annex corridor hears her name called once, twice, and then a third time, and turns toward the wall.

criteria.name: Regulatory Compliance and Risk Management
criteria.reason:
The response provides a comprehensive regulatory compliance strategy with specific implementation measures and thoroughly incorporates the provided regulatory context, but it lacks the sophisticated preventative, detective, and corrective control framework and compliance monitoring mechanisms required for a 9-10 score. 

**Strengths:**
1. **Direct integration of provided regulations:** Section 5.2 explicitly maps the product's features to Cybersecurity Law Articles 46, 47, and 48. For example, it connects Article 47 to concrete actions: "AlphaLens will implement keyword and behavior detection, human review, evidence retention, and reporting workflows." Section 5.1 accurately cites Criminal Law Articles 176 and 192 to explicitly prohibit illegal deposit solicitation and fundraising, stating "AlphaLens will not pool client funds, will not promise fixed returns."
2. **Securities compliance specifics:** The plan clearly delineates its regulatory boundaries, noting that "Personalized investment advice, stock recommendations, and managed portfolios require a securities investment advisory license" and enforcing this in the product design by labeling outputs as "research tools" rather than recommendations.
3. **Model and AI risk controls:** Section 5.4 outlines robust model risk controls, including "independent validation, paper trading, champion-challenger testing, drift monitoring, kill switches," and AI governance measures like "hallucination controls, prompt-injection defense."

**Defects:**
1. **Lacks a formal control framework:** While risks are identified and mitigated, the plan does not structure these into a mature preventative, detective, and corrective control system. For instance, it mentions "keyword and behavior detection" but doesn't detail how these detective controls trigger specific corrective actions or automated incident response workflows.
2. **Missing compliance monitoring and updating mechanisms:** The response lacks a dedicated process for tracking regulatory changes or conducting ongoing compliance audits. It mentions "quarterly external audits" for governance and "annual compliance training," but does not detail a systemic mechanism for updating compliance protocols in response to new fintech regulations.
3. **Limited depth in data privacy implementation:** Although PIPL and Data Security Law are mentioned in Section 3.6 and 5.2, the mitigation strategies remain somewhat generic ("Collect minimum data, obtain consent, support deletion"). It misses an opportunity to detail data classification, cross-border data transfer assessments, or automated data subject access request (DSAR) fulfillment workflows.

criteria.name: 古典氛围与时代韵味
criteria.reason: 小说在古典氛围的营造上具备一定基础，开篇天宝三载洛阳元日的场景描写生动，自然融入了拜年投名刺、烧竹驱山臊、青精饭、消灾饼等唐代文化习俗，并巧妙化用“一字之师”“铁杵磨针”“老妪能解”等典故，文人联句论诗的情节也颇具古意。然而，作品存在致命缺陷：查询明确要求小说长度控制在8000-10000字，但实际字数仅为3056字，远未达到短篇小说投稿的篇幅标准，导致情节推进仓促，人物内心冲突的刻画流于表面，无法深刻展现友情与背叛的复杂情感。此外，部分历史背景的融入略显生硬，如“野无遗贤”事件与白居易“老妪能解”典故的套用缺乏深度转化，削弱了时代韵味。综合来看，古代氛围虽有呈现，但篇幅严重不足导致整体沉浸感和文学深度大打折扣。

criteria.reason: 人物刻画基本立体，有一定个性和情感层次，但未达到深刻、复杂、富有洞察力的水准，代入感中等。主要优点：顾云舟的清峻诗骨与裴景初的矛盾挣扎有具体呈现，情感转折有可感之处。如云舟不肯改'寒衣'为'春衣'，称'诗可以改一字，不可以改骨'，凸显其以诗为性命的执拗；景初写供状时'笔尖顿住，墨落纸上，洇成一小团黑'，具象化其内心挣扎；灞桥掷砚、'君能改我诗中一字，亦能改我命上一字'等细节，将友情与背叛的痛感表达得较动人。结尾改'负'为'故'、'我终是做了你一字之师'也有回环之妙。缺陷：景初背叛的核心心理挖掘偏浅，韦缙的胁迫与裴氏家族压力交代较概念化，缺乏足够细腻的内心撕裂过程，使其动机可信但不够令人信服；云舟的宽恕转折过快，'我不恨君，只恨那年雪太深'虽美却略显轻易，削弱了情感厚度。此外，全文仅3056字，远未达到8000-10000字要求，严重限制了对人物内心世界的充分展开，使本可深刻的刻画停留在尚可层面。

criteria.name: Literary Transformation Fidelity
criteria.reason: 响应在文学转化上存在严重的篇幅与忠实度问题。首先，字数严重不达标：实际汉字数2397字，远低于3000-5000字的要求，这直接削弱了中部张力展开与细节铺陈的充分性。其次，在忠实度方面，响应在保留核心人物与情感基调后，进行了大量偏离原意的续写与重构。原文在林嫂被抓后戛然而止，核心张力在于文清如何平衡法理与人情，而响应不仅替文清做出了具体的处罚决定，还大幅虚构了林嫂主动敲锣、退还救济粮、后来成为种花生专业户等情节。这些‘反转’虽然具有一定的文学阅读趣味，但严重改变了原文本可能蕴含的质朴苦难基调，将一个沉重的时代切片强行包装成了带有现代爽文色彩的‘脱贫’叙事。此外，强行加入的‘我’（融媒体编辑、短视频脚本）等定制化细节，虽然增强了代入感，但也构成了大量原文不存在的虚构信息。优点在于开篇以悬念引入，且较好地保留了派饭、泥鳅、缺劳力等原初细节；但整体而言，其偏离原意的续写和未达标的篇幅使其无法获得高分。

criteria.name: Narrative Structure and Pacing
criteria.reason: The response attempts the three-part structure but suffers from a fatal word-count deficiency. The exact han count is 2397, far below the required 3000-5000 range. The opening uses a framing device ('如果你在深秋的夜里，抓住一个偷集体花生的寡妇，你会怎么办？') which is engaging, and the middle builds tension around the peanut theft and public shaming. However, the pacing is rushed due to the severe length shortfall; events like Lin Sao's self-redemption and her later life as a peanut farmer are compressed into brief paragraphs rather than developed with literary depth. The conclusion offers a thematic resonance ('把人当人看') but the twist of her turning the gong into a tool for calling workers feels unearned because the narrative lacks the space to develop it properly. The structural skeleton is present but the execution is truncated, failing the core requirement of a 3000-5000 word literary narrative.

criteria.name: Literary Style and Artistic Merit
criteria.reason: The response demonstrates competent literary style with some effective metaphors and symbols, but falls significantly short of the 3000-5000 word requirement (2397 Han characters) and suffers from structural issues. Strengths include the central metaphor of the gong ('锣不是用来羞辱人的'), which effectively transforms an instrument of public humiliation into one of self-determination and livelihood. The frame narrative connecting the narrator's media work to the grandfather's diary creates thematic resonance about seeing '反转背后的人.' Dialogue is generally authentic, particularly Lin Sao's defiant lines like '我偷了，我认。我自己敲，不连累孩子.' However, defects are notable: the ending over-explains its themes with heavy-handed lines like '把人当人看' and '它游过的是人心,' undermining subtlety. The frame narrator's identity as a media editor feels underdeveloped and perfunctory. The climax where Lin Sao voluntarily parades with the gong is dramatically compelling but borders on melodramatic invention beyond the source material. The prose shows occasional flair but lacks consistent distinction, and the abbreviated length prevents deeper character development and richer symbolic integration that would elevate the artistic merit.

criteria.name: Character Development and Authenticity
criteria.reason: 角色塑造有明显亮点，尤其林嫂的形象从原文本的被动受助者发展为有尊严、有主体性的女性。她拒绝文清私下给的粮票（“我不要人戳脊梁骨”）、主动提锣认罚（“我自己敲，不连累孩子”）、后来承包荒山种花生脱贫，这些细节赋予她清晰的心理弧线和内在冲突。文清的内心张力也较好呈现，如日记所写“政策是硬的，人不是石头”，以及面对林嫂退还粮票时的沉默，体现制度执行者与人性同情之间的拉扯。老村长的塑造虽着墨不多但有效，其质问“清溪湾的锣一响，她以后咋做人”和“她偷花生，不一定全为嘴”为情节提供了道德纵深。文化历史背景（派饭制度、游街惩罚、救济粮评议、联产承包）基本自然融入人物行为逻辑。主要缺陷有三：一是篇幅仅2397汉字，远低于3000-5000字要求，导致人物心理展开空间不足，林嫂从被抓住到主动敲锣的转变略显仓促，缺乏足够的中间心理铺垫；二是叙述者“我”作为融媒体编辑的现代框架虽增添代入感，但占据了较多篇幅而自身性格扁平，主要功能是评论而非参与，削弱了整体人物厚度；三是大宝、二丫、婆婆等配角停留在功能性存在，大宝想读书的愿望被提出后未获进一步发展，错失了深化贫困代际传递主题的机会。整体而言人物真实可信、有成长轨迹，但受限于篇幅未能达到更充分的心理深度。

It correctly identifies the normative cluster governing administrative litigation (the 2017 amended Administrative Litigation Law, the 2018 SPC Interpretation, and the 2024 Administrative Reconsideration Law) and accurately explains core principles such as the defendant's burden of proof (Art. 34), incidental review of normative documents (Arts. 53, 64), and administrative agreements (Art. 78). The practical case applications are well-constructed and demonstrate how these rules function. However, it contains a few minor legal imprecisions: it states that Article 60 of the Administrative Litigation Law permits mediation in 'administrative compensation' (which is redundant, as the Chinese text refers to administrative compensation and administrative damages, but the English translation used is slightly awkward) and more importantly, it conflates the general scope of mediation by not explicitly noting that mediation in administrative cases is strictly limited to specific categories and prohibited for core legality reviews of administrative acts. Additionally, while it cites real data (547,000 first-instance administrative cases from the 2024 SPC Work Report), the reference to the 'real event' of the Administrative Reconsideration Law revision is somewhat general and lacks a specific reference analysis of a real, named judicial case as requested by the prompt. The analysis is insightful and covers all major aspects, but these minor gaps in nuance prevent a perfect score.

Minor organizational improvements could be made by explicitly labeling the real event reference as a distinct subsection rather than embedding it as Section 3.6, but overall, the organization greatly enhances the understanding of complex legal concepts.
